Boys to Men

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A non-profit company is changing lives... one boy at a time.

Unique Selling Point:
It's called The Character Company and it focuses on creating positive male mentorship for boys with absent fathers. The programme is offered across the country and provides consistent mentoring and safe spaces for boys to develop emotional intelligence. It's an opportunity for South African men to volunteer and become part of the solution of fatherlessness that is so prevalent in South Africa. The non-profit believes much of our country's trauma stems from boys growing up without positive male role models.

Summary:
In South Africa, 60% of children grow up in single parent households. Four out of five boys grow up without positive male role models, according to estimates. Child psychologists believe a boy's entire sense of self can be negatively impacted, without the influence of positive male role models. Depression and aggression are just some of the side effects. Boys can turn to gangsters to provide them with guidance, ending in a cycle of violence. But, The Character Company, is changing this ...one boy at a time. We visit a group of children in Delft, one of the most violent suburbs on the Cape Flats, to meet some of the children being mentored. And we see firsthand, the difference its making in their lives.

Script:


VOXPOP Malachi / 13 YEARS OLD They like to shoot. People get killed.

VOXPOP Lucien / 12 YEARS OLD The two men came in the street. One did shoot. I got shot in my neck.

VOXPOP Christiano / 14 YEARS OLD People shoot here, they throw stones here by the park when children are playing.

VOXPOP Touhir / 12 YEARS OLD My mother’s friend woke me up and told me they stabbed my father. And that was really sad for me.

CLIP 309 boy puts head in his hands

UPSOUND (under visuals) Raymond Weaver “Delft is a very impoverished area. Basically what they did is dumped the people here and left”.

CUT TO BLACK

VO 1 This is Delft - a place where childhood years are far from magical.

VO 2 Here, survival is an everyday challenge. On the outskirts of Cape Town, it has one of the highest murder rates in the country.

VO 3 Most of the children growing up here live in single parent households. Boys with absent fathers… easy prey for gang recruitment.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk / The Character Company Founder: Four out of five boys do not have a positive male role model. The numbers are staggeringly high. It also has no boundaries, there’s no district for this. There’s no municipal zone where this will happen. It’s across the board.

VO 4 Jaco van Schalkwyk is trying to change that. He started the non-profit organisation, the Character Company, eleven years ago.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: The desire for us is to see every boy has got someone he can connect with, that’s going to say you’ve got what it takes, you’re good enough let’s do this.

NATSOUND (Day 2 / Cam 1 / Clip 284) 00:12 “Nice one, nice intercept there”

VO 5 Jaco himself grew up without a father.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: There’s an uncertainty you walk around with that attracts bullying, so I got very badly bullied. 06:42 I grew up in an environment where sport was very important. I was the only boy in the school who took typing so that did not help. So all of these things played a role in low self-esteem.

VO 6 He realised he could use his own experiences to help others, and founded The Character Company to provide positive male role models to boys.. Mentors giving guidance when fathers are absent.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: So we’ve got what we call FAT guys. Faithful, available and teachable. And these are mentors we pull into the space. We screen them, we vet them, it’s a long process they have to go through. We really make sure these men are men of quality and the kind of men we want to help raise the next generation.

LINK: This is more than just a programme. It’s a nationwide movement. Volunteers across the country are changing lives and giving boys the guidance they need.

VO 7 Social worker Edith Kriel has been working with children for the past thirty years, and she’s seen the consequences of growing up without a father, firsthand.

UPSOUND Edith Kriel / Jelly Beanz Executive Director: We’re looking at poor self esteem, poorer academic performance and in time poorer economic opportunities and ability to take care of themselves and family. 02:01 What we sometimes see particularly with boys is when there is pain on the inside, they often show it on the outside. Hurt people hurt people.

VO 8 She says without a father to model behaviour on, boys struggle to express themselves emotionally.

UPSOUND Edith Kriel: We’re looking at boys not able to always know their strength, how to use their strength in either a hurtful or helpful way.

VO 9 Edit works with children who have suffered trauma, abuse and neglect. And it’s common to have an absent father.

UPSOUND Edith Kriel: We’re looking approximately at sixty percent of children growing up without their biological fathers present in their lives. And that has a huge impact on how children grow, how children develop. And how they navigate their world.

VO 10 For Jaco, the work The Character Company does is about prevention - boys between the ages of five and twelve are given mentorship before the negative consequences of having an absent father set in.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: Our next generation, our young men need this, they are hurting and they are bleeding and we have to put some plasters on that.

NATSOUND Children praying

VO 11 Raymond Weaver is one of The Character Company’s mentors filling that gap - working with boys as young as five years old.

NATSOUND Clip 312 Time code 00:22 What is our five values?
00:36 “Respect, honesty, courage, kindness, self-discipline”.

VO 12 Groups of usually no more than five boys meet with their mentor once a week.

UPSOUND Raymond Weaver / The Character Company Mentor: Why must we be kind to people who aren’t kind to us? Why is it important to show them kindness too? (SUBTITLE)
CLIP 317 Respek vir die ander mense (subtitle)
Raymond “Daarsy” (Subtitle)

VO 13 These boys, as they enter their teen years, are vulnerable to negative influences around them.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: High school is where the biggest need for connection starts. How do I find the place where I belong? And that’s often where it goes wrong. With regards to gangs, bad friendships, substance abuse, all the stuff we medicate with, it starts there.

VO 14 For Raymond, this work is about setting these boys on the right path before it’s too late. A meeting with a suicidal teenager several years ago, validated his decision to dedicate his life to changing the lives of young boys.

UPSOUND Raymond Weaver: He said I can’t live with myself anymore. He told me he shot about 30 people and he killed five.

MAC: 11:31 A fifteen year old boy?

UPSOUND Raymond Weaver: He told me this story how I’ve seen my father killed in front of me, he lives around the corner, since five years old and I told myself I’m going to get them back, he grew up with that hatred in my heart. And when Jaco came on board and I told him that story, he said just imagine you had that boy since five years old under your wing, do you think he would have done all those things. And that was a lightbulb moment for me.

VO 15 For the past year, he’s been working with these boys, and he’ll be there for them for years to come.

UPSOUND Raymond Weaver: Cape Town is one of the most beautiful cities in the world and some of these children never even saw Table Mountain. Some of them never even saw the beach. When I took one of them to the beach, he asked me where does this dam come from (laughs) 00:41 For them, this is the world. This is where it ends. (photos whatsapped to you)

VO 16 Mentors use outdoor activities… and humour .. to connect with the boys in weekly interactions..

VO 17 And the changes… are …evident.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: You see boys come into the programme, low self-esteem, struggling at school, and suddenly we’re filling those gaps. And a year later, we’re class captain, play well at sport, photos and we celebrate those things. And you can see the changes in that.

MAC AND RAYMOND AND BOYS PLAYING BALL

LINK: Jeez, I thought I was fit. You know just being with these boys and playing with them reminds me of what I do with my kids sometimes when we just have lots of fun together. As a father, this is what is important because it’s what builds bonds, and makes you a present dad.

VO 18 And its the being present, that makes all the difference. Because even if there is a father in the home, if he doesn’t interact, the consequences are the same as having an absent father.

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: When you have a father that lives in the house where you are present, you are kind of reminded twice a day that you are not good enough. When you wake up in the morning and he’s not there, or he’s there and he doesn’t spend time with you, that’s a constant reminder that there’s something wrong with me, cos if it wasn’t surely he would spend time with me.

VO 19 While we were filming in Delft, there was another shooting, another young life lost. Violence here has become such an everyday occurrence, that it drives home just how important the work is that The Character Company does .

UPSOUND Jaco van Schalkwyk: We have a solution, we see this work. We see boys being mentored, we see boys being removed from the statistics on gender based violence, and substance abuse and corruption. Clip 262 / Day 1 Time code 14:06 If we don’t do this our boys end up in prisons and graveyards at an alarming rate.

VO 20 As the shadows lengthen, signalling the end of another afternoon with Raymond, the boys gather for a group hug - it’s the way they always end their meetings.

NATSOUND Clip 341 / Day 2 Time code 00:37 Moenie huil nie, next week kom ek weer (subtitles).

VO 21 It’s hard to say goodbye - but Raymond will be back, as he promised. He’ll show up for them…as he always does.
